summary: This standards-track document describes methods for carrying PostScript in both MIME and X.400 mail systems and for converting between them.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes two X.400 body-part forms for PostScript and how they correspond to MIME's application/postscript type. The bytes can be copied between the forms without conversion.

how is postscript carried in x400
what is the x400 postscript ftam body part
does postscript conversion change the bytes
subtitle: Two X.400 carriers for PostScript and their mapping to MIME application/postscript.

tldr.problem: Mail systems need defined ways to carry PostScript in X.400 and map it to MIME.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes an Extended Body Part and an FTAM Body Part, each mapped to application/postscript without conversion.
tldr.outcome: The RFC recommends the FTAM method; both representations carry a single octet stream.

today: RFC 2160 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: PostScript in Two Mail Systems
sections.content:
The document describes methods for carrying PostScript in MIME and X.400, and for converting between the two mail systems. It describes an X.400 Extended Body Part and an FTAM Body Part.

The RFC recommends the FTAM method.
sections.plainLanguage: The document gives two ways to carry PostScript through X.400. It recommends the FTAM body part.

sections.title: The X.400 Body-Part Forms
sections.content:
The Extended Body Part postscript-body-part has no parameters and carries an OCTET STRING. Its identifier is { mixer-bp-data 2 }. The PostScript FTAM Body Part is identified by an application-reference whose identifier is { mixer-bp-data 6 }.

The Extended Body Part carries forward work originally defined in RFC 1494.
sections.plainLanguage: Each X.400 form has a different identifier. Both carry the PostScript content as a stream of bytes.

sections.title: MIME Mapping and Security
sections.content:
MIME carries PostScript as application/PostScript. The RFC maps both X.400 forms to application/postscript with no conversion because both contain a single stream of octets.

The RFC says PostScript security issues are discussed in RFC 2046 and adds no new security issues. It also notes that PostScript is a trademark of Adobe Systems, Inc.
sections.plainLanguage: The same byte stream is used on both sides, so the gateway copies it without changing it. The memo adds no new security rules.

references.text: Kille, S., "MIXER: Mapping between X.400 and RFC 822/MIME", RFC 2156, January 1998.
